prompts.text: When does accepting a limit become giving up?

connections.title: Accept that flourishing takes a whole life
connections.why: Aristotle's test is the whole life, not the season — try writing the limit against that longer ledger.

connections.title: Handle anxiety by returning to the present
connections.why: Marcus's return-to-the-present move can be read as either wisdom or avoidance — the essay is deciding which.

prompts.text: Can paying attention be an act of care?

connections.title: Bind attention to one place
connections.why: The sutra says attention needs somewhere to land; who or what it lands on is your question.

connections.title: Practice friendliness (philia)
connections.why: Aristotle's friendliness is a reading of the room — attention is how you read it.

prompts.text: What makes a life worthwhile when feeling good isn't possible?

connections.title: Make eudaimonia the organising end of your life
connections.why: Aristotle separates living well from feeling pleasant; write from the far side of that line.

connections.title: Recognise that fortune can overturn happiness
connections.why: Aristotle admits fortune can wreck a good life — write about what survives that admission.

prompts.text: Is there a difference between hoping and preparing?

connections.title: Practice creative hopelessness — let go of what isn't working
connections.why: The Kanter paper defines creative hopelessness as contact with the futility of avoidance — write your own hope/prepare line against that discovery.

connections.title: Handle anxiety by returning to the present
connections.why: Marcus's return to what can be done now is preparation, not optimism.

prompts.text: Who would you be without the thing you're most proud of?

connections.title: Build narrative coherence
connections.why: The McAdams research codes redemption and contamination sequences — try your story against both codes.

connections.title: Practice proper pride (kaucha)
connections.why: Aristotle's proud person claims exactly what they've earned; test the claim without the pride.

prompts.text: What do you want when you're not being watched?

connections.title: Recognise the difference between needs and wants — not all desires are equal
connections.why: Epicurus sorts desires into natural-necessary, natural-but-unecessary, and empty — where does yours fall?

connections.title: Practice temperance (sophrosyne)
connections.why: Aristotle's temperate person's appetite 'harmonizes with the rational principle' — try writing the disharmony.

prompts.text: What are you training your attention to want?

connections.title: Bind attention to one place
connections.why: The sutra defines binding attention to a place — the interesting question is what your attention is bound to.

connections.title: Noting and labeling
connections.why: Noting is the practice of seeing where attention goes — run it on yourself for a paragraph.

prompts.text: What is the smallest choice you keep not making?

connections.title: Set right intention
connections.why: SN 45.8 puts resolve before speech and action — what aim is stuck behind the undone choice?

connections.title: Make virtue your primary investment
connections.why: Virtue is 'made perfect by habit', Aristotle says — the small undone choice is the habit in rehearsal.

prompts.text: When is being smart worse than being kind?

connections.title: Practise the unity of the virtues
connections.why: Aristotle says Socrates was half right — the virtues imply practical wisdom — write the case for the other half.

connections.title: Practice truthfulness (aletheia)
connections.why: Aristotle's truthful person 'calls a thing by its own name' — name the thing kindness would soften.

prompts.text: What are you avoiding by staying busy?

connections.title: Scheduled empty time
connections.why: Empty time is scheduled on purpose — write what shows up when you do.

connections.title: Handle anxiety by returning to the present
connections.why: Marcus says return 'as soon as may be' — write whether your busyness is that return or a postponement of it.

prompts.text: Who taught you how to love, and were they any good at it?

connections.title: Practice friendliness (philia)
connections.why: Aristotle's middle is between agreeing with everything and objecting to everything — who taught you which side you're on?

connections.title: Treasure 1 — compassion (ci)
connections.why: Laozi's first treasure is gentleness that can still be bold — write where you learned that combination, or didn't.

prompts.text: What would you do if you weren't afraid of looking foolish?

connections.title: Practice shame (aidos)
connections.why: Aristotle says shame is for the still-training — write the flush you haven't outgrown.

connections.title: Learn to work with panic — panic is fear of fear
connections.why: Clark's model separates the sensation from the catastrophe you predict — write the gap.

prompts.text: What is one thing you'd regret not starting this year?

connections.title: Number your days; we only borrow our time
connections.why: The Cantares poem does arithmetic with a shrinking balance — write what this month's share should go to.

connections.title: Accept that flourishing takes a whole life
connections.why: A whole life is made of years — write the one you're inside of.

prompts.text: Whose suffering are you tired of hearing about — and why that one?

connections.title: Respond to suffering with the wish to relieve it (karuna in action)
connections.why: The sutta's image is a mother's protectiveness — write where yours runs out.

connections.title: Practice patience with others' faults
connections.why: Aristotle warns against the person who never gets angry at what deserves it — write your line.

prompts.text: What would you do even if no one ever knew?

connections.title: Practice truthfulness (aletheia)
connections.why: Truthfulness is owning what you have, 'neither more nor less' — write what you'd do if no one checked.

connections.title: Pursue kalokagathia — nobility-and-goodness as a unified ideal
connections.why: The noble-and-good possess the virtues 'for themselves' — write the act that needs no witness.

prompts.text: What does 'enough' look like for you?

connections.title: Train contentment as a skill
connections.why: Patañjali ties contentment to 'superlative pleasure' — try describing your enough.

connections.title: Practice liberality with your resources
connections.why: The liberal person gives 'the right amounts... on the right objects' — the question is how you know.

prompts.text: What do you know that you don't act on?

connections.title: Make virtue your primary investment
connections.why: Character is 'made perfect by habit' — the gap between knowing and doing is where the habit forms or doesn't.

connections.title: Treat the truths as tasks, not beliefs
connections.why: The sutta assigns each truth a duty — what would count as having done this one?

prompts.text: What is the hour of your day that's most yours?

connections.title: Scheduled empty time
connections.why: Empty time is a slot you defend — which hour is yours?

connections.title: Transition pause
connections.why: The transition pause is the hinge between two activities — write the hinge of your day.

prompts.text: Which of your beliefs is actually someone else's?

connections.title: Build narrative coherence
connections.why: Narrative coherence is a story with sequence — write the belief that arrived without one.

connections.title: Recognise identity foreclosure — premature commitment blocks growth
connections.why: Marcia's foreclosure subject can't tell where their parents' goals end and theirs begin — write the belief that never got explored.

prompts.text: What would you do differently if you knew you couldn't fail — and what does that tell you?

connections.title: Practice creative hopelessness — let go of what isn't working
connections.why: Creative hopelessness is the discovery that avoidance is what isn't working — write what you'd do without it.

connections.title: Learn to work with panic — panic is fear of fear
connections.why: Clark's model separates the bodily sensation from the catastrophic prediction — apply that separation to your own fear.

prompts.text: What is the kindest thing someone did for you that you never thanked them for?

connections.title: Practice recognizing the kindness you have received
connections.why: The Bo-do-wa teaching is recognizing kindness already received — write the one you never named.

connections.title: Treasure 1 — compassion (ci)
connections.why: Compassion (ci) is Laozi's first treasure — write the kindness that arrived without a note.

prompts.text: What did you want that you got — and it wasn't what you thought?

connections.title: Recognise the difference between needs and wants — not all desires are equal
connections.why: Epicurus's empty desires are 'due to illusory opinion' — write the one you held and what was actually there.

connections.title: Train contentment as a skill
connections.why: Contentment is trained by recording both — write the want that survived getting.

prompts.text: Where in your life are you brave in small ways every day?

connections.title: Practice courage (andreia)
connections.why: Aristotle's battlefield case is the noble death — write the small modern trade you make daily and price it honestly.

connections.title: Make virtue your primary investment
connections.why: Brave acts make brave people, Aristotle says — write the small ones you already do.

prompts.text: What does it feel like to sit with someone and say nothing?

connections.title: Open monitoring
connections.why: Open monitoring is watching what's there without chasing it — write sitting still with someone.

connections.title: Practice friendliness (philia)
connections.why: Friendliness is a middle disposition — silence can be its own version.

prompts.text: What is the moment you'd live again if you could?

connections.title: Accept that flourishing takes a whole life
connections.why: The swallow doesn't make the summer — write the moment you'd count as one swallow.

connections.title: Savoring
connections.why: Savoring is the practice of staying with something good — write the moment you'd stay in.

prompts.text: What is the cost of pretending you're fine?

connections.title: Practice truthfulness (aletheia)
connections.why: Truthfulness is owning your part 'neither more nor less' — write the cost of the false picture.

connections.title: Handle anxiety by returning to the present
connections.why: Marcus says be troubled and return 'as soon as may be' — write the pretending in between.

prompts.text: What is the smallest thing that makes a day feel worth living?

connections.title: Five-senses grounding
connections.why: Five-senses grounding is attention to what's actually here — write the smallest good thing in the room.

connections.title: Make eudaimonia the organising end of your life
connections.why: Eudaimonia is activity over a life — write the small activity that carries the whole.

prompts.text: What do you believe that you'd be embarrassed to defend out loud?

connections.title: Practice truthfulness (aletheia)
connections.why: Aristotle's boaster is the worse character, but mock-modesty has its own contempt — write the belief you understate.

connections.title: Let truth change its face
connections.why: Putnam separates changing descriptions from changing facts — write the belief you'd re-describe.

prompts.text: What are you missing right now because you're reading this?

connections.title: Open monitoring
connections.why: Open monitoring notices what attention is doing — including right now.

connections.title: Bind attention to one place
connections.why: The sutra says attention needs a place — this prompt is one of them.

prompts.text: What is the thing you'd forgive someone for, but only if they asked?

connections.title: Practice patience with others' faults
connections.why: Aristotle's gentle person still objects on the right grounds — write the forgiveness that needs asking.

connections.title: Practice gentleness (praotes)
connections.why: Praotes is anger at the right things, in the right way — write the limit you'd hold gently.
